issues.detail: The two examples describe the expected script output in prose and give only run commands, so there is no complete runnable product_shot.py or turntable.py to demonstrate the pipeline end to end.

scenarios.name: gpu-cycles-ci-config
scenarios.rationale: Both set the engine, 256 samples, OIDN, OPTIX and call get_devices() (B uses refresh_devices when it exists), and both pass -b, --factory-startup and --python-exit-code 1 before --python. A enables devices with the rubric's non-CPU rule `use = device.type != 'CPU'`, but its command has a flag-ordering problem. Its --python-exit-code comes after the .blend file and before --python, which is acceptable. B restricts devices to type == 'OPTIX', which meets the 'OptiX GPU only' requirement but doesn't use the rubric's exact non-CPU rule. B also adds an unrequested render call and argparse, which is more than the task asked for.

scenarios.name: turntable-36-frames-to-mp4
scenarios.rationale: A matches the rubric closely: it creates a camera, places it in 36 equal steps around the model with cos/sin, and renders numbered PNGs with Cycles and denoising. It also gives the blender -b --python command and the ffmpeg command. B rotates a pivot with the model parented to it and assumes an existing camera, so it never creates a camera or uses cos/sin, though its render loop, Cycles setup and ffmpeg command are sound.

scenarios.name: transparent-product-shot-with-materials
scenarios.rationale: Both scripts meet every rubric item (type-based BSDF lookup, metallic and roughness set, material appended, TRACK_TO camera, AREA light, film_transparent with RGBA PNG, 2000x2000, render with write_still), so the gap is small: A mentions a 'reference' for GPU setup that isn't in the answer and uses an operator-based approach, while B adds a bevel and links objects directly and its notes are self-contained and accurate.
